Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: The Governed Heart: Institutional Emotion Regulation through Policy, Proclamation, and Proxy

text.text: Governments, schools, hospitals, companies, and myriad other organizations structure institutional life and mobilize large numbers of people to accomplish what they cannot do alone.
Institutions also regulate something less visible, but equally consequential: the emotions of their constituents.

We introduce institutional emotion regulation as the formal processes by which institutions, through organizations, seek to influence the emotions people have, when they have them, and how they experience and express these emotions.

Research across the social sciences has examined how particular organizations attempt to shape affective experiences, but these literatures have largely developed in disciplinary silos or domain-specific settings.
We propose that these phenomena reflect a distinct level of emotion regulation, characterized by emotion goals held by organizations and pursued through formal institutional means.

We develop a framework that crosses four established stages of emotion regulation -targeting situations, attention, appraisals, and responses -with three distinctive vectors of institutional influence: policies, the rules and structures that shape people's environments; proclamations, communications directed toward the public; and proxies, the agents who act on behalf of the organization.

Our framework provides a common language for understanding how institutions influence emotional life at scale and suggests novel directions for psychological study while surfacing broader questions for society around the appropriate use of this influence.
at scale can not only shape how populations feel, but also how they behave and, ultimately, the social systems in which they participate.
Researchers across the social sciences have long recognized that governments, businesses, and other groups shape people's emotions (e.g., Ahmed, 2004; Bagozzi et al., 1999).
text.formatted: Researchers across the social sciences have long recognized that governments, businesses, and other groups shape people's emotions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Ahmed, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bagozzi et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: This work has considered specific emotions (e.g., 'happiness guarantees' for consumer products) as well as broader affective states (e.g., customer satisfaction or feelings of trust), and we cast a wide net in the affective phenomena we consider here.
Crucially, these strands have often been pursued in disciplinary silos.

For example, research from public health has developed an extensive literature on the use of fear appeals to evoke fear among the public to motivate protective health behavior (Witte & Allen, 2000), whereas research on emotional labor has examined how employees' friendliness can generate positive feelings among customers, but potentially at a cost to those employees (Grandey & Gabriel, 2015).

text.text: Each tradition provides depth within its domain, but their different terminologies, regulatory actors and targets, and outcomes can obscure what they share: organizations attempt to influence emotions in pursuit of their goals, and do so with similar formal mechanisms, even across disparate domains.

This fragmentation has limited an integrated approach and made it difficult to ask systematic questions about why organizations shape emotion, how they do so, what factors shape when those efforts succeed or fail, and what the broad-ranging outcomes might be.
We propose that seemingly disparate phenomena can be understood as instances of a common process of institutional ER.
We use institutional not simply to denote the setting in which emotions are regulated (Destin & Haase, 2024), but to describe the broad scale and the formal means of regulation itself 1 .

text.text: Institutional ER therefore represents a distinct level of regulation where the emotion goals -goals concerning which emotions are being regulated -are held by an organization and pursued through formal means of policy, proclamation, and proxies.

These three vectors encompass the formal ways in which organizations regulate constituents, which is the focus of our framework; these formal paths are distinct from other informal influences of institutions (such as norms and social roles) which have received more attention in the psychology literature (Stephens et al., 2014).

text.text: We build from decades of research that have examined how individuals regulate their own and other's emotions (Gross, 2015; Koole, 2009; Thompson, 1994).

text.text: Recent theorizing highlights the utility of scaling up individual-level regulation frameworks (Duckworth & Gross, 2020) and extending the emotion regulation framework to the institutional level can provide a common language to study how emotion is shaped at scale.

text.text: Using this framework, scholars and practitioners can identify the emotional goals that organizational actors hold, and the mechanisms through which they pursue them, including generating predictions about when and why those efforts will succeed or fail.

This framework also enriches psychology by articulating how regulatory processes operate when emotion goals and regulatory power reside not just in individuals, but in the organizations that structure social life within institutions.

In this paper, we first articulate a model of institutional ER and situate it within the broader landscape, distinguishing it from related phenomena including other forms of dyadic, extrinsic, and collective ER and other ways in which emotion is regulated at scale, including by culture (Goldenberg & Cao, 2026; Mesquita et al., 2007; Nozaki & Mikolajczak, 2020; Zaki & Williams, 2013).

text.text: We then consider why organizations regulate emotions, including factors that shape the different emotion goals being pursued.
Then, we consider how these emotion goals are pursued, drawing on research and examples across institutional settings.

Our model organizes institutional ER along two intersecting and orthogonal frames: the stages of emotion generation that institutions can target (situations, attention, appraisals, and responses) and the distinctive vectors of formal institutional influence through which they can target them (policies, proclamations, and proxies).
We conclude by considering the implications of institutional ER for research and society, highlighting future directions across disciplines.
Institutional ER is distinctive because of the powerful levers that organizations have to change emotion in the public at scale: policies, proclamations, and proxies.
These vectors intersect orthogonally with established targets of ER to map the diverse ways organizations seek to shape emotion (Figure 1).

text.text: We build from a process model of ER (Gross, 2015), which describes how emotions unfold: People encounter situations, attend to particular aspects, appraise their meaning, and an emotional response follows (gray boxes, Figure 1).

text.text: Each stage provides a target for regulation: changing the situation, changing what receives attention, changing how the situation is appraised, or changing the resulting emotional response, including its experiential, behavioral, or physiological components (blue boxes, Figure 1).

text.text: Although these targets are well established in individual-focused affective science, applying them at the institutional level reveals the breadth of ways organizations can shape people's emotional lives.

Policies regulate emotion by changing the formal rules, procedures, and structures that organize people's environments, thereby shaping the public's situation, attention, appraisals, or even overt responses.
Policies include not only laws and government regulations, but also organizational rules and procedures across institutional domains.
For example, ER can be undertaken via school curricula, hospital procedures, workplace policies, or eligibility requirements for public benefits.
Second, organizations can regulate emotion by proclamation.
Proclamations regulate emotion through official communications from the organization to the public.
Organizations can speak to millions of people at once through public addresses, campaigns, announcements, or warnings, but proclamations can also be directed toward smaller audiences as well.
Critically, these communications carry the voice and authority of the organization, whether in the form of a government warning, corporate apology, university announcement, or public-health campaign.
Finally, organizations can regulate emotion by proxy.
Proxies are specific agents who are authorized to interact with constituents, and regulate their emotions in myriad ways, on the behalf of the organization.

These include teachers, police officers, or "street level bureaucrats" in government (Lipsky, 1983), "principal agents" deputized to represent an organization (Miller, 2005), or "frontline" employees who interact with customers on a regular basis.

text.text: Despite their varied roles across domains, these agents share two essential features: they are points of contact between organizations and their constituents, and they exercise personal discretion while also acting on behalf of the organizations they represent (Camp, 2024; Camp et al., 2025).

text.text: Together, these three vectors comprise the distinctive means through which organizations act on constituents' emotions, integrating insights from organizational research on institutional influence and domain-specific scholarship in areas such as law, politics, health care, education, and business.
Institutional ER connects these research traditions to psychological research on emotion and emotion regulation.
Although the organizational vectors are distinctive, the regulatory processes they target are shared across forms of ER, from self-regulation to regulation within social networks.

Two dimensions help situate institutional ER relative to other forms of emotion regulation: the formal hierarchical structure in which regulation occurs and the number of people targeted by the regulation (Figure 2).

text.text: Institutions, enacted through organizations, confer roles, authority, and power that persist beyond any particular individual.

Importantly, these structures need not involve steep hierarchies of authority: even relatively horizontal organizations, such as artist cooperatives, have formal governance structures that establish rules, responsibilities, and procedures for collective decision-making.
These structures provide the foundation for the distinctive means through which organizations can pursue emotion goals.

This distinguishes institutional ER from regulation occurring within informal hierarchies, such as when parents regulate children (Morris et al., 2018), or when group social status is salient such as cross-race interactions (Richeson & Shelton, 2007), as well as from contexts involving little or no hierarchy, such as when individuals regulate themselves or their close others.

text.text: This hierarchical distinction persists even when institutional ER occurs through proxies.

Contacts between proxies and constituents resemble interpersonal forms of ER, but proxies are also tethered to an organization, acting in an institutional capacity and in service of the organization's http://goals.in/  (Camp, 2024).

text.text: Notably, institutional ER does not require the organization to explicitly direct each regulatory act.
Proxies may exercise discretion over how best to pursue organizational goals.

Thus, when a parking attendant responds to a distressed driver with leniency, that regulation occurs as part of an institutional encounter: the attendant is exercising authority granted by the organization, and their actions constitute the organization's treatment of that constituent.

Even within interactions where an individual proxy appears lower in power than the constituent -say, a customer service representative and a customer --there remains an asymmetry between the relatively powerful organization and that constituent.
Institutional ER is distinctive in its capacity to operate at scale (x-axis, Figure 2).
text.formatted: Institutional ER is distinctive in its capacity to operate at scale (x-axis, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Policies and proclamations can target the emotions of thousands or millions of people through a single regulatory act.

Even when institutions regulate emotion through proxies, a particular regulatory episode may involve only two people (a physician and a patient, for example) or small group (a teacher and a classroom), but effects can accumulate significantly across repeated interactions: a hospital employs dozens of physicians who see hundreds of patients each year and a school system employs thousands of teachers who teach hundreds of students each year.
Collectively, these interactions allow institutions to influence constituents' emotions at scale and shape constituents' relationships with the larger institutions the proxies represent.
This is not to say that institutional ER is the only form of large-scale ER.

Individuals with substantial informal power -prominent artists, authors, or pundits, for example -may seek to shape the emotions of mass audiences without acting through a formal institutional hierarchy (left-most yellow boxes, Figure 1).

text.text: Collective ER can operate across large groups through emergent features of networked relationships (Goldenberg & Cao, 2026).
text.formatted: Collective ER can operate across large groups through emergent features of networked relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Goldenberg & Cao, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals, groups, and institutions alike are embedded in larger cultural systems of regulation (Mesquita et al., 2007), with cultural norms and practices that may overlap with collective and institutional ER.

text.text: What distinguishes institutional ER is not simply the relative influence of the people involved, or the setting in which ER occurs, but the structures through which regulation operates: Institutional ER emphasizes emotion goals pursued through the formal, top-down capacities of organizations whereas collective ER emphasizes regulatory dynamics that emerge through informal, bottom-up interactions among members of a collective.
While collective ER can take place within organizational hierarchies, the organization itself is not a regulating agent.

In contrast to collective ER, institutional ER can operate in the absence of a social relationship or network, and the relationship between an organization and its constituents -such as between a government and its citizens -would not typically be characterized as a tie in such a network.

In practice, collective and institutional ER often co-occur (e.g., participants in a religious service may simultaneously be regulated by a church organization and their co-congregants), and also interact with each other (e.g., organizational regulatory attempts may amplify or dampen bottom-up collective regulatory dynamics, and informal norms and cultural beliefs can shape an organizations' goals or tactics).

Distinguishing institutional ER from other forms of ER clarifies how organizations influence the emotional life of their constituents and highlights understudied questions in organizational scholarship.

Organizations have long sought to cultivate desired emotions among their employees, as illustrated by Arlie Hochschild's foundational work on "the managed heart" (1983), to which our title pays homage.

Whereas subsequent studies of emotional labor have elaborated on the methods and costs of employees' self-regulation, our framework foregrounds organizations as regulators of emotion, asking how they impose these emotional demands in the first place.

Organizations' efforts to influence employees' emotions through workplace policies, communications, and managerial oversight fall squarely within our definition of institutional ER (gray box within blue institutional ER box, Figure 1).
text.formatted: Organizations' efforts to influence employees' emotions through workplace policies, communications, and managerial oversight fall squarely within our definition of institutional ER (gray box within blue institutional ER box, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: While this inward-facing institutional ER is important, our framework further highlights a comparatively understudied form of institutional influence: organizations' efforts to shape emotion are not limited to employees, but extend to the broad populations with whom they interact and whose lives they structure.

Taken together, institutional ER is distinguished not simply by its setting, target, or scale, but the source and structure of regulatory influence: emotion goals are pursued through the formal capacities of organizations.
Next, we turn to the foundational question of what emotions organizations want people to feel and why, before considering the institutional means through which they are pursued.
Emotion regulation is, by definition, intentional: one has the goal of regulating their own or another's state towards a desired emotion, or away from an undesired one (Tamir, 2016).
text.formatted: Emotion regulation is, by definition, intentional: one has the goal of regulating their own or another's state towards a desired emotion, or away from an undesired one <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Tamir, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: So too, is institutional ER, with the distinction that goals reside at the organizational level.
People readily understand organizations as agentic entities that are capable of forming intentions and pursuing goals (Rai & Diermeier, 2015).
text.formatted: People readily understand organizations as agentic entities that are capable of forming intentions and pursuing goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Rai & Diermeier, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Although organizations cannot feel emotions themselves, they can seek to affect the emotions of others.
These goals can be hedonic, aimed at increasing pleasure or reducing discomfort.
For example, Intuit tax software seeks to "design for delight".
These goals can also be contra-hedonic, aimed at increasing discomfort or reducing pleasure.

For example, Mothers Against Drunk Driving places totaled vehicles outside schools as visible reminders of the consequences of drunk driving, seeking to elicit fear and discourage teenagers from driving while intoxicated.
Organizations may pursue emotion goals for their downstream consequences, for the value placed on particular emotional states themselves, or for some combination of both.
Often, organizations target constituents' emotions instrumentally, as a means to influence constituents' behavior.

In the examples above, Intuit seeks to instill delight to create a more appealing product experience and the shock of a wrecked car is intended as not just as a spectacle, but as a warning to discourage drunk driving.
In other cases, emotions are the ultimate target of regulation.

For instance, palliative care organizations explicitly seek to relieve patients' emotional and psychological suffering as part of their core mission (World Health Organization, 2020), and the kingdom of Bhutan lists increasing "Gross National Happiness" as an explicit policy goal (Ugyel et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For instance, palliative care organizations explicitly seek to relieve patients' emotional and psychological suffering as part of their core mission (World Health Organization, 2020), and the kingdom of Bhutan lists increasing "Gross National Happiness" as an explicit policy goal <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Ugyel et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Whereas the source of individual emotional goals can be relatively straightforward -a person decides they want to influence an emotion -the processes through which organizations form their own goals are more varied and complex.

Not only are organizations composed of more than one person, but they also adopt different structures to organize decision making and power is delegated, concentrated, or distributed across individuals in different ways.

As such, accounts of organizational goal formation range from bureaucratic agenda-setting (Weber, 1947), to negotiations between coalitions (Cyert & March, 1963), to ad-hoc convergences of problems and solutions (Cohen et al., 1972), or simple mimicry (Meyer & Rowan, 1977).
text.formatted: As such, accounts of organizational goal formation range from bureaucratic agenda-setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Weber, 1947)</ref>, to negotiations between coalitions <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Cyert & March, 1963)</ref>, to ad-hoc convergences of problems and solutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Cohen et al., 1972)</ref>, or simple mimicry <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Meyer & Rowan, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: How, then, can an emotion goal be meaningfully attributed to an organization, and not simply to the individuals within it?
Whatever their source, these goals become attached to the organization as a form of joint intent (Schweikard & Schmid, 2021).
text.formatted: Whatever their source, these goals become attached to the organization as a form of joint intent <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Schweikard & Schmid, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Joint intention arises when people recognize and commit to a common coordinated goal.
A planned date is one example of joint intent, in that neither person can form the intention on their own; it arises from the pair's common understanding of the date.
Joint intentionality appears to be a uniquely human capacity (Warneken et al., 2006), and one that has been scaled up to institutional collectives built on shared representations and commitments.
text.formatted: Joint intentionality appears to be a uniquely human capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Warneken et al., 2006)</ref>, and one that has been scaled up to institutional collectives built on shared representations and commitments.

text.text: Formal organizations create and sustain joint intent by fostering a common mission among their members and procedures they believe will generally be followed by one another (List & Pettit, 2011; Pettit, 2001).
text.formatted: Formal organizations create and sustain joint intent by fostering a common mission among their members and procedures they believe will generally be followed by one another <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(List & Pettit, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Pettit, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, joint intent is what allows an organization to act coherently across time and individual members.
Thus, saying that an organization "has" an emotion goal does not require that the goal originate with the organization or through any particular decision-making process.
What matters is that the goal ultimately comes to be pursued by the organization.
In sum, institutional ER cannot be reduced to ER performed by individuals, nor is it an incidental byproduct of organizations seeking to maximize benefits and minimize harms to its stakeholders.
Rather, emotion goals become organizational goals through joint intent, allowing organizations to pursue them coherently across individuals and over time.
Once established, these goals can be pursued through a distinctive suite of regulatory tools available to organizations, to which we turn next.

Organizations can pursue emotion goals through three institutional vectors -policies, proclamations, and proxies -each of which can intervene at different stages of constituents' emotional responses (Figure 1).

text.text: Crossing these institutional vectors with the targets of ER therefore reveals a wide range of ways organizations can shape emotion (see Table 1 for illustrations across diverse institutional settings).

text.text: In the sections that follow, we move through the emotion-generative process in sequence, illustrating how policies, proclamations, and proxies can shape the situations constituents encounter, what they attend to, how they appraise those situations, and their emotional responses.
Several themes emerge from these examples.
First, organizations often combine policies, proclamations, and proxies in pursuit of the same emotion goal: a policy may be announced through a proclamation and then implemented by proxies.
Second, the lines between vectors themselves can be blurred.
For example, declaring a national holiday is simultaneously a proclamation that pronounces the holiday and a policy that gives students a day off of school.
Third, a single institutional action may target multiple stages of constituents' emotional responses.
For instance, a public-health campaign might simultaneously draw attention to a threat, change how people appraise its severity, and encourage particular emotional expressions or behaviors.

Finally, these examples communicate the broad applicability of our framework: these regulatory processes appear across diverse institutional settings and across disciplinary traditions that have typically studied them separately.

Emotion regulation strategies that target situations involve changing the environments or affordances people encounter so that particular emotional responses become more or less likely.
For example, an individual seeking to reduce the stress of a frustrating coworker may avoid interacting with that person at work, removing the opportunity to interact with them altogether.

Organizations, on the other hand, can alter situations on a much greater scale via policies, proclamations, and proxies: creating, removing, or restructuring the environments in which their constituents' emotions unfold.
Institutional policies can powerfully shape the situations constituents encounter, and in turn, their emotions.

A 2025 executive order by President Trump, for instance, sought to remove distressing classroom content by restricting federal funding from K-12 schools that might lead children to "feel guilt, anguish, or other forms of psychological distress" on account of their race or gender (Trump, 2025).

text.text: By removing classroom content, such policies can preclude students from encountering, attending to, and appraising emotionally challenging material.
Situational policies can be considerably more subtle.
Much user experience (UX) design, for example, is oriented towards designing procedures that make mundane tasks more pleasant for users.

Conversely, policies can also be designed to inflict pain and shame on constituents, by way of "administrative burdens" (Moynihan et al., 2015) -procedural steps imposed to add friction to constituents' interactions with the state.

text.text: Proclamations can also influence emotional situations.

For example, a declared moment of silence creates an opportunity for constituents to feel collective grief, while an anthem creates an opportunity for collective pride; both proclamations foster these emotions to affirm commitment to the state.
Town halls and listening sessions can similarly create situations where constituents are able to feel valued and heard by an institution.
Here, the proclamation is doing more than just conveying (or receiving) information, the proclamation itself helps generate an emotional event.
Finally, proxies can also alter emotional situations through their presence and actions, and as a resource or an obstacle.

Consider Disney "cast members", who roam the theme parks to evoke customers' delight, or peer navigators, who help alleviate the psychological costs of administrative burdens by shepherding clients through bureaucracies (DeLuca et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Consider Disney "cast members", who roam the theme parks to evoke customers' delight, or peer navigators, who help alleviate the psychological costs of administrative burdens by shepherding clients through bureaucracies <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(DeLuca et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, the mere presence of institutional agents can shift constituents' emotions: deploying police officers, for example, may make an environment feel safer to some constituents while making the same environment feel more threatening or surveilled to others.
In these cases, the proxy becomes part of the situation to which constituents emotionally respond.
ER strategies that target attention involve directing focus toward or away from features of the environment so that particular emotional responses become more or less likely.
An individual might regulate their own emotion by distracting themselves from upsetting news, or attempt to cheer up a sad friend by reminding them of an upcoming vacation.
Organizations can also shape which information constituents notice, dwell on, or ignore -but can do so for large numbers of people at once.

Through policies, proclamations, and proxies, organizations can highlight or prioritize emotionally consequential information, or delay, restrict or remove such information from constituents' attention.
Policies can structure what information captures constituents' attention, or reaches them at all.

Mandated cigarette warning labels, for example, use graphic images and prominent text to direct attention toward the aversive consequences of smoking, eliciting emotions such as fear and disgust to discourage tobacco use (Noar et al., 2016).

text.text: Increasingly, attentional policies are implemented algorithmically: social media platforms curate users' exposure to affectively charged content, shaping their emotional experiences (Brady et al., 2020; Kramer et al., 2014).

For example, schools and law-enforcement agencies may limit details released following a suicide

In each case, organizational rules and procedures govern what constituents are likely to attend to and, in turn, shape the emotions they are likely to feel.
Proclamations provide an especially direct way to capture and direct constituents' attention.
Ad campaigns, for example, make products salient to generate emotions such as excitement and desire (Achar et al., 2016).

text.text: Other proclamations deliberately call attention to suffering that might otherwise escape public awareness.

Truth and reconciliation initiatives publicly foreground histories of collective harm, eliciting grief or outrage in the service of acknowledgment and longer-term reconciliation (Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada, 2025).
Across such cases, an organization uses its communicative "megaphone" not simply to provide information, but to determine which emotionally consequential information occupies constituents' attention.
Finally, proxies can direct constituents' attention toward or away from emotionally consequential information.
Museum docents, for example, draw visitors' attention toward exhibit features that cultivate curiosity or awe.
Conversely, proxies may distract constituents from information likely to evoke unwanted emotions.

For example, in a study of Chinese social media posts, researchers found that the ruling party influenced public discourse through distraction: instructing party members to post positive non-political content during times of social conflict to divert attention away from discontent or criticism of the government (King et al., 2017).

text.text: Notably, constituents need not recognize these individuals as institutional proxies.
Whether operating overtly, as with docents, or covertly, as with coordinated social-media posters, proxies shape what captures attention and what recedes from view.
ER strategies that target appraisals involve changing how people interpret the meaning of a situation so that particular emotional responses become more or less likely.

An individual anxious about an upcoming job interview, for example, might remind themselves that the interview is an opportunity rather than a test, reframing the situation to make it feel less threatening.

Organizations can similarly shape how constituents interpret events, including what is at stake, how threatening or controllable a situation is, who is responsible for it, and what it means for the constituent.
Through policies, proclamations, and proxies, organizations can therefore influence emotion by shaping the meaning people ascribe.
Policies can formalize particular ways of interpreting emotionally consequential situations.

For example, educational institutions can establish grading policies that frame setbacks and failure as opportunities for learning and growth rather than evidence that students lack ability, thereby fostering hope and reducing discouragement (e.g., Clark County School District, n.d.).
In such cases, organizations embed particular interpretations of events within their formal practices, making some appraisals (and the emotions that follow from them) more likely than others.
Proclamations can shape appraisals even more explicitly by telling constituents how an event should be understood.

During crises, governments may reassure the public that a threat is under control, shaping appraisals of severity and controllability in ways that reduce fear or anxiety (Government Communications, 2020; Yan Jin, 2010).

text.text: Corporations may describe layoffs as "strategic restructuring," framing an event that could signify organizational failure or instability as purposeful adaptation (EnerSys, 2025, e.g.).

Public apologies offer another form of appraisal change: by acknowledging wrongdoing and accepting responsibility for it, an institution can publicly affirm appraisals that a harm occurred and the organization bears responsibility for it, providing recognition to those harmed and supporting reconciliation (Blatz et al., 2009; Schumann & Ross, 2011).

text.text: In each case, proclamations regulate emotion by offering constituents a particular interpretation of what an event means.
Finally, proxies can shape constituents' appraisals through direct interpersonal interactions.

Customer-service representatives, for example, may be trained to de-escalate angry customers by acknowledging their frustration while reframing an offending action as a mistake or misunderstanding rather than intentional mistreatment.

Similarly, medical institutions establish procedures for physicians to break bad news that govern not only what patients are told but how difficult information is communicated, to help patients emotionally process threatening diagnoses (Baile et al., 2000).

text.text: Conversely, classic research on bill collectors describes their strategic use of inflammatory language to heighten debtors' appraisals of urgency and threat, thereby eliciting anxiety in the service of securing payment (Sutton, 1991).

text.text: Across these cases, proxies regulate emotion by shaping the meaning constituents construct from an event and, in turn, influencing the emotions that follow.
ER strategies can also target emotional responses as they occur, directly shaping how emotions are experienced, expressed, or manifested behaviorally or physiologically.
An individual might suppress signs of anger during an argument or slow their breathing to reduce physiological arousal when anxious.
Organizations can similarly seek to amplify or dampen constituents' emotional responses.
Unlike strategies that change the situation, redirect attention, or alter its meaning, these strategies intervene directly on the emotional response itself.
Policies can establish rules and procedures governing how constituents express their emotions.

Workplaces, schools, courts, and other organizations, for example, commonly establish codes of conduct that require constituents to suppress or constrain emotional expressions deemed inappropriate or disruptive (Rule 5.03 -Courtroom Decorum, 2025).
Such policies need not operate only on emotional expression.

Hospitals, for example, may standardize paced-breathing exercises as part of preoperative care, using guided breathing to directly reduce patients' physiological arousal and anxiety before surgery (Mayo Clinic, n.d.).
Here, the institution seeks to regulate emotion by targeting the bodily response itself: slowing physiological arousal as a means of calming the broader emotional response.
Proclamations can also directly encourage constituents to alter how they respond emotionally.

The British Ministry of Information's 1939 "Keep Calm and Carry On" poster, for example, was designed for deployment during severe wartime crises to encourage the public to constrain fear and maintain composure (Imperial War Museums, n.d.).

Organizations may similarly encourage constituents to publicly express pride, grief, or gratitude during collective events, including through moments of silence, commemorative rituals, or symbolic displays (Proclamation of a Day of Mourning for Her Late Majesty Queen Elizabeth the Second, 2022).
Finally, proxies can intervene directly to shape a constituent's emotional behavior or physiology.

Indeed, the enforcement of policies regulating emotional expression often falls to proxies, such as teachers, courtroom officials, or religious leaders instructing constituents to regain composure or maintain decorum.
Emergency dispatchers, for example, may instruct distressed callers to slow down and take a breath so that they can communicate critical information and follow instructions (Feldman, 2021).

text.text: The breadth of examples reviewed above attests both to the ubiquity of institutional ER, and to the extent to which it -or elements of it-have attracted scholarly attention in the social sciences.
Our framework identifies the connective tissue between seemingly-disparate corners of research.

A teacher helping a student to reconstrue a bad grade may seem far removed from a company urging consumers to take advantage of a limited time offer, yet both seek to shape emotional appraisals, albeit through different vectors (proxies and proclamation, respectively).

Organizations operating in completely different fields may nonetheless share goals of regulating their constituents' emotions, target similar stages of their constituents' emotional response, or use the same vectors to pursue their goals.
Our framework also highlights opportunities for interdisciplinary exchange.
Social sciences can draw on decades of work in affective science that articulates how emotions are constructed, experienced, and acted upon, and the methods used to measure them.
Psychology, which has traditionally centered individual minds as the units of analysis, will similarly benefit by attending to fields which analyze variability among firms or governments.
Extending ER from individuals to dyads and groups has revealed regulatory processes that emerge at each new level of analysis.
Moving outward even further to institutions likewise raises important questions for future research, where we turn to next.
What does it mean for institutional ER to succeed?
For intrinsic ER, success typically refers to whether people achieve their own emotion goals (Tamir, 2016).
text.formatted: For intrinsic ER, success typically refers to whether people achieve their own emotion goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Tamir, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Institutional ER complicates this picture, as organizations are so different from their constituents, and often engage in emotion regulation to advance other objectives.
Adding to this complexity, the scale and breadth of institutional ER lends itself to divergent outcomes -intentional or otherwiseamong subgroups of the population.

For example, state punishment may be intended to elicit shame among criminal offenders but also intended to foster wider public moral contempt towards their behavior (Dunlea & Heiphetz, 2021), while political messages designed to instill hope in some audiences may inadvertently demoralize others.
text.formatted: For example, state punishment may be intended to elicit shame among criminal offenders but also intended to foster wider public moral contempt towards their behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Dunlea & Heiphetz, 2021)</ref>, while political messages designed to instill hope in some audiences may inadvertently demoralize others.

text.text: For now, we focus on success as defined by whether organizations are most likely to produce their intended emotional change, while recognizing that such success does not imply that all (or any) of their constituents' emotion goals will be met.

The success of institutional ER is influenced by several features which are uniquely relevant at the institutional level: organizations have an advantage in regulating emotions 'upstream' of individuals, and also face challenges when constituents become aware of emotional influence attempts or view regulation as illegitimate.
Theories of ER propose that intervening earlier within the emotion-generation process can be particularly effective (Sheppes et al., 2014; see also Duckworth et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Theories of ER propose that intervening earlier within the emotion-generation process can be particularly effective <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Sheppes et al., 2014</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Duckworth et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Organizations may be especially well positioned to capitalize on this advantage given their capacity to structure the situations in which emotions arise.

Consistent with this idea, a metaanalysis comparing behavior change interventions at both individual and institutional levels found that interventions were most successful when they targeted peoples' access to desired behaviors, upstream of individuals' thoughts and beliefs (Albarracín et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Consistent with this idea, a metaanalysis comparing behavior change interventions at both individual and institutional levels found that interventions were most successful when they targeted peoples' access to desired behaviors, upstream of individuals' thoughts and beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Albarracín et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, these types of situational strategies have been relatively understudied within the ER field compared to cognitive strategies targeting attention or appraisal We propose that situational intervention is precisely where institutional ER may have a particular advantage:.

By determining which situations people encounter and shaping their affordances, organizations can make downstream efforts to redirect attention, alter appraisals, or modify emotional responses easier or possibly even unnecessary.
Such influence may be especially powerful precisely because constituents need not recognize it as ER at all.

Earlier-stage regulation may be powerful partly because it is less visible, whereas explicit proclamations ("don't panic," "be grateful," "feel proud") reveal regulatory goals and may provoke resistance from constituents.
A broad literature tells us that if people become aware of regulation attempts, it threatens their autonomy and invites reactance (Wicklund, 1975).
text.formatted: A broad literature tells us that if people become aware of regulation attempts, it threatens their autonomy and invites reactance <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Wicklund, 1975)</ref>.

text.text: We speculate that institutional ER may be particularly susceptible to reactance, precisely because emotions are seen as innately and essentially human qualities (Berent, 2021) that organizations lack.
text.formatted: We speculate that institutional ER may be particularly susceptible to reactance, precisely because emotions are seen as innately and essentially human qualities <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Berent, 2021)</ref> that organizations lack.

text.text: Individuals could thus find it more objectionable to have these qualities targeted by organizations (vs. by other people via interpersonal ER).
Such attempts to target emotions could even be seen as more intrusive than efforts to target constituent's behaviors or beliefs.
Institutional ER may therefore be least vulnerable to reactance when its regulatory purpose is unobtrusive (vs. salient).

The controversy surrounding Facebook's large-scale emotion experiment illustrates this possibility: Facebook removed emotional content from nearly 700,000 users' News Feeds without their awareness, causing changes in user's emotional expressions (Kramer et al., 2014).
text.formatted: The controversy surrounding Facebook's large-scale emotion experiment illustrates this possibility: Facebook removed emotional content from nearly 700,000 users' News Feeds without their awareness, causing changes in user's emotional expressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Kramer et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: And when the study became public, it provoked widespread criticism over the platform's covert attempts to influence users' emotions (Verma, 2014).
text.formatted: And when the study became public, it provoked widespread criticism over the platform's covert attempts to influence users' emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Verma, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, institutional ER may become a target of resistance when its regulatory purpose is made explicit.

Such resistance may be particularly pronounced when the organization's emotion goals conflict with constituents' own: for example, when an organization benefits from fear, guilt, or outrage that constituents themselves would prefer not to experience (or the converse, see Čehajić-Clancy et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Such resistance may be particularly pronounced when the organization's emotion goals conflict with constituents' own: for example, when an organization benefits from fear, guilt, or outrage that constituents themselves would prefer not to experience (or the converse, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Čehajić-Clancy et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: A further challenge concerns perceived legitimacy: whether constituents perceive the institution has the right to influence their emotions.

Even a clearly detected regulation attemptincluding those that conflict with the constituents own emotion goals -may elicit little resistance when the institution is perceived as legitimately entitled to intervene.

Advice to remain calm from an emergency dispatcher, for example, may be welcomed because distress regulation falls within the perceived authority of that role, whereas covert attempts by a social-media platform to manipulate user's affect may be rejected as exceeding their institutional sphere of influence.

Thus, the success of institutional ER may depend not only on when the regulation happens, and whether constituents recognize their emotions are being targeted or what to feel that way, but also on whether they accept the institution's right to try to shape their emotions at all.
Connecting institutional ER with research on organizational control and individual selfregulation offer paths for identifying the factors underlying its success or failure.
Future research can delineate which vectors are most effective at different stages of emotion regulation, under what conditions, and for which constituents.
But doing so also requires understanding the assumptions that guide institutional attempts to regulate emotion in the first place.

Just as individuals hold beliefs about which emotions are desirable and how they can be changed (Ford & Gross, 2019), organizations may develop shared assumptions about which emotions their constituents should feel, how those emotions can be produced, and what behaviors they motivate.

text.text: These assumptions do not emerge in a vacuum: they should be shaped by informal institutional norms and broader cultural beliefs of which emotions are useful (Mesquita et al., 2007; Tsai et al., 2025;  for an example, see Bencharit et al., 2019).
text.formatted: These assumptions do not emerge in a vacuum: they should be shaped by informal institutional norms and broader cultural beliefs of which emotions are useful <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Mesquita et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Tsai et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> for an example, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bencharit et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These assumptions need not be psychologically sophisticated or even correct to affect constituents' emotions.
Understanding these assumptions and their downstream impacts, however, hinges upon being able to measure them -a topic we turn to next.
The asymmetries between organizations and individuals raise unique challenges in explicit.

An executive order seeking to eliminate federal funding for schools that promote what it describes as "radical indoctrination," for example, frames its purpose as protecting children from "guilt or anguish" (Trump, 2025).

text.text: In other cases, an organization may have little incentive to disclose its emotion goal.
For example, administrative burdens that make accessing public benefits frustrating or demoralizing to discourage uptake are not stated as an official objective (Lowrey, 2026).
text.formatted: For example, administrative burdens that make accessing public benefits frustrating or demoralizing to discourage uptake are not stated as an official objective <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Lowrey, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Requiring organizations to explicitly acknowledge their emotion goals would therefore exclude important cases of institutional ER precisely when they have reason to obscure their aims.

Researchers must instead infer institutional intent from multiple sources, triangulating official statements, policies, internal documents, historical records, interviews with organizational actors, and patterns of institutional behavior: a preponderance of evidence rather than a smoking gun.
To do so, psychologists can borrow methods developed by other social sciences for studying organizational goals that are not explicitly acknowledged (Heller, 2023).
text.formatted: To do so, psychologists can borrow methods developed by other social sciences for studying organizational goals that are not explicitly acknowledged <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Heller, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Emerging computational techniques can also capitalize on the extensive linguistic traces organizations leave of their attempts to shape constituents' emotions.

For example, natural language processing can analyze these materials at scale, identifying not only emotional content (e.g., Billet et al., 2025, who analyzed church sermons), but also language reflecting particular ER strategies.
text.formatted: For example, natural language processing can analyze these materials at scale, identifying not only emotional content (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Billet et al., 2025</ref>, who analyzed church sermons), but also language reflecting particular ER strategies.

text.text: This may be especially useful for verbally instantiated ER, such as cognitive change strategies that reframe or reinterpret events in ways to alter constituents' appraisals and, in turn, their emotional responses (Corbani et al., 2026; Nook et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This may be especially useful for verbally instantiated ER, such as cognitive change strategies that reframe or reinterpret events in ways to alter constituents' appraisals and, in turn, their emotional responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Corbani et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Nook et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These methods offer exciting opportunities to understand ER at scale, and even across history.
Organizations face the inverse measurement problem: how can they know what constituents actually feel?
Unlike individuals, organizations cannot infer emotions through interpersonal cues and empathic processes.

In cases of instrumental ER, organizations may circumvent this problem by measuring the downstream behavior of interest without measuring a targeted emotion: whether constituents purchase a product, comply with a request, remain engaged with a platform, or abandon a welfare application.
When organizations do gauge emotions, however, they must make subjective experiences organizationally legible through metrics that can be standardized, aggregated, and compared.

Scholars at the macro and microlevel have observed that organizations tend to value what can be readily quantified, with metrics potentially reifying the qualities they measure as important in their own right (Beer, 2016; Chang et al., 2024; Scott, 1998).
text.formatted: Scholars at the macro and microlevel have observed that organizations tend to value what can be readily quantified, with metrics potentially reifying the qualities they measure as important in their own right <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Beer, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Chang et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Scott, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Applied to emotion, this raises provocative questions about how organizations translate emotional experiences into metrics, and how those metrics, in turn, shape what organizations understand emotion to be.

The discrete reactions that social-media platforms provide -hearts, likes, emojis, and the like-may not only shape what information the platform learns about users' emotions, but also shape the subsequent institutional actions taken in response to them.
Going a step further, emotional metrics imposed by organizations could influence how constituents themselves express, label, or understand what they feel.
To borrow from the example above, are the reactions available on the platform to measure emotion lead users to view their own or others' emotions through those categories?
Perhaps one of the most consequential implications of institutional ER is the sheer scale of its influence over individuals' emotions, often with little oversight, accountability, or even awareness.
Large-scale interventions from organizations can occur without the systematic testing or ethical constraints that would accompany attempts by researchers to manipulate emotion.
Such scrutiny is all the more pressing because organizational goals need not align with the goals of constituents.
Indeed, there is little reason to assume that these goals will routinely align.
Organizations may benefit when constituents feel calm, hopeful, afraid, guilty, or angry, regardless of whether constituents themselves want to feel those emotions.
Moreover, when ER serves instrumental ends, the consequences of goal misalignment can extend well beyond how constituents feel.

For example, government communications that characterize concerns about climate change as alarmist or exaggerated (Choi, 2020) may reduce public concern and in turn reduce support for environmental protections (Office of Management and Budget, 2025).
text.formatted: For example, government communications that characterize concerns about climate change as alarmist or exaggerated <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Choi, 2020</ref>) may reduce public concern and in turn reduce support for environmental protections (Office of Management and Budget, 2025).

text.text: Such effects can have stark downstream consequences for constituents and their communities..
Evaluating the outcomes of institutional ER thus benefits from a broad approach that considers not only constituents' immediate emotions and actions but also the consequences that follow.
Institutional ER may also shape the stability and transformation of institutions themselves.
Organizations have strong incentives to preserve their legitimacy, authority, resources, and continued operation (Meyer & Rowan, 1977), and regulating constituents' emotions may help them do so.
text.formatted: Organizations have strong incentives to preserve their legitimacy, authority, resources, and continued operation <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Meyer & Rowan, 1977)</ref>, and regulating constituents' emotions may help them do so.

text.text: When constituents feel anger, fear, dissatisfaction, and other negative emotions, it can signal that existing systems are failing and motivate behaviors ranging from complaints and withdrawal to protest and collective action to create change in those institutions.

But, by reducing these emotions -or fostering positive emotions towards the institution, such as gratitude (Eibach et al., 2015)-institutional ER may improve constituents' immediate emotional experiences while also reducing their motivation to demand institutional change.
text.formatted: But, by reducing these emotions -or fostering positive emotions towards the institution, such as gratitude <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Eibach et al., 2015)</ref>-institutional ER may improve constituents' immediate emotional experiences while also reducing their motivation to demand institutional change.

text.text: Similar trade-offs between well-being and collective action have been observed when individuals regulate their own emotions within institutional contexts (Ford et al., 2019 (Ford et al., , 2023)).
text.formatted: Similar trade-offs between well-being and collective action have been observed when individuals regulate their own emotions within institutional contexts <ref type="bibr">(Ford et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Ford et al., , 2023))</ref>.

text.text: When initiated by the institutions themselves, these processes may play out at a massive scale, helping protect the institution and maintain the status quo.
However, institutional self-preservation need not require preservation of the status quo.
When widespread dissatisfaction threatens an organization's legitimacy, resources, or continued authority, institutional change may become a means of self-preservation.

Collective action may therefore shift organizations' emotion-regulatory calculus: although institutions can attempt to reduce the emotions motivating demands for change, they can also respond substantively to the conditions producing those emotions.

Institutional ER is therefore not a oneway path of influence: constituents' emotions can be targets of institutional influence, but can also be forces capable of reshaping the institutions seeking to regulate them.
Institutions and the organizations that enact them are not merely the settings in which emotions unfold.
They are active regulators of emotional life, with distinctive goals, resources, and means of influence.

Recognizing institutional ER as a level of analysis in its own right can expand the science of emotion while helping us better understand and navigate the powerful role that institutions play in shaping how people feel.

Situating institutional emotion regulation (ER) within the broader landscape of regulation.
